title: Being a meat proxy for AI should be grounds for getting people fired
excerpt: Devs using AI as a way to escape responsibility for the code they push is hurting software engineering and should be stopped.
content_html:
Published on 08 Nov 2026

I generally avoid ranting in this blog, but the issue I'll cover today is genuinely pissing me off. I apologize in advance for the more aggressive tone that this post will have because I think it's necessary in this case to get the point across.

When someone is assigned a task, be it to review a PR, work on a reasonably complex coding task, or even just asked a simple question, and all they do is prompt an agent "do X" and copy-paste the results back to you, with zero guidance or validation on behalf of the human (meaning it was 100% handled by the agent), and oftentimes failing to disclose or actively attempting to hide the fact that the work was fully AI generated, this should in my opinion be seen as an attempt to scam the company and be treated just as severely as other software engineering job scams. It should result in the developer receiving a warning and even the threat of possible termination of employment in more serious cases and if the dev fails to comply.

I've chatted with many colleagues who have had experiences with teammates behaving like this, and one common question that is raised when this topic is brought up is: "Isn't all work supposed to be AI generated nowadays? Are they really in the wrong if you consider that?". But there's a huge difference here. I'm not talking about the usual AI-assisted workflow which is commonplace nowadays where the human guides the agent, corrects it, reviews what comes out of it and opens PRs based on something that has been properly validated and cleaned up for other humans to review.

I'm talking about a specific scenario that has become worryingly common over the last few months where the human was simply a meat proxy between you and whatever agent they used, meaning that the presence of the person added no value and you would've been better off launching an agent yourself and skipping them entirely. They might have even potentially made things worse for you by acting as a proxy, and in more egregious cases even intentionally attempted to hide this fact and/or used it as a way to strip themselves of any responsibility regarding the code they write and merge (e.g. "This code broke master and took down production? It was opened and merged under my user? No, you see, it's not my problem because it was the AI who did this, not me!").

This behavior is becoming increasingly prevalent in the software engineering industry and it's damaging it. I think this behavior should be punished because devs who do this are:

  • Wasting your time, because if all they do is proxy their work to an agent, you might as well skip the person and do that yourself
  • Forcing you to do their work for them, because you now have to not only review and validate agentic output that they did not, but also potentially have to be one dealing with the consequences of any nonsense code that they may have managed to merge when you were not paying attention
  • Wasting the company's time and resources, as this behavior is basically a convoluted way of stating that they are 1) getting paid a salary to do nothing of value, 2) harming the company's products (more on that below), and 3) wasting the time of anyone having to deal with them, particularly when the dev intentionally tries to hide their actions and pass AI generated output as their own words or code

It's essentially a novel way to silently scam the company and colleagues and is in my eyes no different than other known software engineering scams such as covertly having two jobs or hiring a third-party to do your work for you and act as if they were you while you do something else.

I always saw the software engineering field as being comprised of two groups of people: people who are devs because they are passionate about building software, and people who don't actually enjoy software but joined the field because it's a job that pays well. The latter being something that I find to be a perfectly fine thing to do as long as, you know, you actually do your job. Pre-AI, although sometimes I've found people in this group to not have been doing a particularly impressive job, they were still doing it nonetheless. So things were fine then.

But now that AI is widespread, I've been bumping into many folks who basically weaponized AI to make it seem like to their managers they are being extremely productive by opening hundreds of PRs with very complex descriptions and bold claims of having fixed major issues and/or greatly improved systems, when in reality a deeper look reveals that this "work" is actually just a bunch of unreviewed vibe-coded nonsense that not only doesn't fix or improves anything at all, but also actively harms whatever products they are "working" with and massively complicates the work of the devs who have to deal with the consequences of said garbage code and actually care about building good products and using AI responsibly.

This is getting so insane that I've even had cases where I would DM someone on Slack and notice right away that I'm talking to an AI. Not in the sense that they've set up an agent to handle their messages for them (wouldn't be surprised if people start doing this though), but that they are copying my question to an agent and pasting back the response (without disclosure, so making it seem that they wrote it themselves). WTF?

Some colleagues suggest that a way to fight back is to throw AI back at the person (so if you get a barrage of unreviewed AI-generated review comments on your PR, throw another unreviewed AI-generated barrage of AI responses back at the person). But I feel that this just makes everything worse. It may get the PR itself out of your hands, but the code will suffer as a result and you'd still have to end up dealing with the consequences of that.

I don't understand why someone who doesn't like their job would try so hard to come up with ways to not do it that they would be fine with messing up their colleagues' work in order to achieve it. Nobody is forcing anyone to work in tech. If someone doesn't like it, they can just quit and do something they actually enjoy. It's what I would've done at least if I was in their situation.
